subject: Behavioral Economics
title: The Self-Serving Bias
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Self-Serving Bias.

hook.text: Students who ace exams credit hard work. Students who fail blame unfair questions. Same class.

buildup.text: We attribute success to our own effort and talent but blame failure on outside circumstances.

discovery.text: Self-serving bias protects self-esteem. Taking credit feels good. Accepting blame threatens identity.

twist.text: In team projects, every member estimates their own contribution above 25%. The totals exceed 100%.

climax.text: This bias keeps us confident but blind. Growth requires owning failures, not just victories.

punchline.text: You won because of you. You lost because of them.

quiz.question: What does the self-serving bias cause in team projects?
options: Everyone estimates their own contribution as above average

details.summary: The self-serving bias is the tendency to attribute successes to personal ability and effort while blaming failures on external circumstances. This pattern protects self-esteem but prevents learning from mistakes by externalizing the causes of poor outcomes.
details.whyItMatters: The self-serving bias undermines personal growth, organizational learning, and fair attribution. When people take credit for success but blame luck for failure, they never develop the self-awareness needed to improve their performance systematically.
takeaways: People attribute successes to skill and failures to external factors
The bias protects self-esteem but prevents learning from mistakes
It creates asymmetric accountability in organizations

faq.question: How does the self-serving bias affect teams?
faq.answer: Team members take credit for group successes and blame others for failures. This creates conflict, erodes trust, and prevents accurate post-mortem analysis. Each person sees their contribution as central to success and peripheral to failure.

faq.question: Is the self-serving bias universal across cultures?
faq.answer: It is weaker in collectivist cultures where modesty norms encourage attributing success to the group and accepting personal responsibility for failures. Western individualistic cultures show the strongest self-serving attribution patterns.
